original_question: When a non-reduced scheme X occurs as the eigenscheme of a tensor, what degrees can the irreducible components of X have, and which schemes can appear as such irreducible components?
target_in_paper: Section 2.1, Problem 10: the open problem on non-reduced eigenschemes of symmetric tensors, posed as a specialization of Problem 9 on eigenconfigurations.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual statement and almost paraphrases Problem 10. It correctly focuses on a non-reduced eigenscheme X, asks about the possible degrees of its irreducible components, and asks which schemes can occur as irreducible components.
missing_details: The paper is in the symmetric-tensor setting here: X is the eigenscheme of a symmetric tensor, equivalently of a homogeneous polynomial f in S^dV, not of an arbitrary non-symmetric tensor (Section 2.1, p. 6).
The ambient field is the complex numbers: the paper’s standing notation says it mainly works over C unless stated otherwise (Notation, p. 2).
The eigenscheme is a projective subscheme X_f of P(V), not just an abstract scheme (Section 2.1, p. 6).

The definition of eigenscheme should be stated: X_f is defined by the condition \nabla f(v) \wedge v = 0; equivalently, by the 2 x 2 minors of the matrix with first row x_0, ..., x_n and second row \partial_0 f, ..., \partial_n f, where x_0, ..., x_n are coordinates on V and \partial_j = \partial/\partial x_j (Section 2.1, p. 6).

The nearby context is specifically about finite, hence 0-dimensional, eigenschemes: Problem 10 is introduced as a specialization of Problem 9 on the variety of eigenconfigurations E_{n,d}, viewed inside Hilb_{D_{n,d}}(P(V)) (Section 2.1, p. 6).

To make the question stand-alone, the quantifiers should be explicit: one ranges over all dimensions n+1 = dim V, all degrees d >= 2, and all symmetric tensors f in S^dV whose eigenscheme X_f is finite and non-reduced (Section 2.1, pp. 6-7).
Because the relevant eigenschemes here are 0-dimensional, the degree of an irreducible component is its scheme-theoretic degree, i.e. its length; your draft leaves this implicit.
The paper adds a benchmark case that helps fix scope: for matrices (d = 2), all schemes arising as irreducible components of an eigenscheme are known to be curvilinear (Problem 10 context, p. 7).

There is no nilpotency hypothesis or 'for all sufficiently large m' clause in this problem; the hidden assumption to surface instead is finiteness/0-dimensionality of the eigenscheme in the Problem 9 to Problem 10 transition.
refined_question: Over \mathbb{C}, fix a vector space V with dim V = n+1 and an integer d >= 2. For a symmetric tensor f in S^dV, viewed as a degree-d homogeneous polynomial, let X_f \subseteq \mathbf{P}(V) be its eigenscheme, defined by \nabla f(v) \wedge v = 0 (equivalently, by the 2 x 2 minors of \begin{pmatrix}x_0&\cdots&x_n\\ \partial_0 f&\cdots&\partial_n f\end{pmatrix}). Assume that X_f is finite and non-reduced. Which integers can occur as the scheme-theoretic degrees (lengths) of the irreducible components of X_f, and which 0-dimensional schemes can occur as irreducible components of such eigenschemes?
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 2.1 on eigenschemes of symmetric tensors, and its wording is nearest to the paper’s official formulation in Problem 10. The surrounding text defines eigenschemes only after identifying a symmetric tensor with a homogeneous polynomial f in S^dV, places the eigenscheme inside projective space P(V), and introduces Problem 10 as a specialization of Problem 9 on eigenconfigurations in the Hilbert scheme of points. Those nearby definitions make symmetry, homogeneity, projective ambient space, and finiteness/0-dimensionality the main implicit assumptions that must be restored to make the question fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper.
